title: Do u guys think it’s worth switching to three js?
author: _Vultrix_
selftext: Seeing a lot of fable 5.2 content online with three js showing some very nice procedural content which is making me wonder if it’s a better approach then normal 3d asset workflows using blender or tripo in unity/unreal. So I’m contemplating whether switching to it is a better idea mainly for environment/scene creation, not so much for characters. Although it could be that those scenes online take huge amounts of money and tokens and it’s cheaper to use 3d assets, I’m not sure.

comments.author: StoneCypher
comments.body: three is the right choice if you're deploying on the web.  it won't work on consoles.  it's a pain in the ass on phones.  in steam, there's a good argument to be had, and it's one viable choice among many.  there isn't much of a difference in terms of 3d support

comments.author: redditscraperbot2
comments.body: Depending on how far you intend to develop your game, three.js might turn into more of a hindrance than a help, but for short one off affairs its pretty good.

replies.author: _Vultrix_
replies.body: So three js is not as strong for larger games?

replies.author: redditscraperbot2
replies.body: It absolutely can do them, but it can get messy quick and asset management becomes difficult.

comments.author: Pik-cher
comments.body: Since you're weighing it for environments, I'd try a small three.js scene before committing. Ask your coding agent for one procedural room or terrain patch and see how it looks and runs, since that tells you more than the demos online. In my experience with browser games, the costs that bite are draw calls and mobile performance, so ask it to reuse geometry and keep the lights simple. If you only need static environments for a Unity or Unreal project, regular 3D assets are probably still the easier route.

replies.author: _Vultrix_
replies.body: I see, I will try it, for me personally what makes procedural appealing is that it’s way easier to edit if u change ur mind about stuff

comments.author: Pleasant_Salt6810
comments.body: depends on your game and use case, some games can be very good in three js, but some are not. it's really a usecase question.

comments.author: blueeetherabbit
comments.body: if you're making an online game I would keep it as far away from any webstack as you can. If it's a single player game sure, use whatever stack is easy

comments.author: count023
comments.body: I use three.js for a rapid prototyping and for the smaller projects, it's faster of rme to test 3d based games and get results than to bash it all out in unity for a prototype that doesn't work

replies.author: amunozo1
replies.body: How costly and hard is to migrate things from the threejs prototype to Unity?

comments.author: atastycrow
comments.body: just try it dude. you can spend liquidity half a day getting on boarded and see if it works

comments.author: riccioverde11
comments.body: Yes Queen serve your slop hot and steamy

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I personally can't see much of a difference. You can always do a Web build of your Unity game. 

I started doing my games in purely Three.js, and have some good results. But lately I've found Unity is letting me get some things done quicker. 

One issue you will come across is how do you edit levels? I ended up writing my own Unity style editor to let me hand craft levels. And at that point realised I was basically recreating Unity. 

I think it depends on whether you want to use existing assets from the Unity store. I've got a huge collection I've bought over the years, and my AIs can browse it to find suitable assets. You'll need to do a little bit of fix ups to get those working in Three.js, and some asset licences may not allow you to use them outside of Unity. 

It does let you get deep down into the rendering, but you've really got to build everything from scratch - including basic stuff like colission and player controllers. Claude can do most of it, though with older models I really could struggle to get it to work like a regular game engine. Opus 5.5 seems to do pretty well, but it still needs a fair bit of guidance to get the feel right.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
You are comparing apples to oranges to bananas.

UE is a game engine.

Blender is a modelling tool with an underlying rendering engine.

three.js is a high level graphics API.

They all do different things and serve different purposes.

three.js gives you less, not more, which is probably why you can more efficiently one-shoot prototypes that LOOK good. If that's all you want, have fun. It doesn't help with making an actual playable game and working on it iteratively.

You can also use three.js or play webgl for prototyping visuals you will later integrate into your actual game. Whether this beats Bldnder is up to you to find out.
